title: The Coke Ovens to One East Seventieth Street: Frick, the Lockout, and the Pictures
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: West Overton and the Coke Ovens

stops.name: West Overton, born in the springhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinates given in the research pool placed the birth some twelve kilometres northeast of the Overholt homestead and are corrected here to the West Overton site
stops.campa: A second child of six is born to John W. Frick and Elizabeth Overholt Frick in the springhouse on the Overholt property at West Overton, East Huntingdon Township, Westmoreland County. His mother's father, Abraham Overholt, owns the mill, the distillery, and the coal under the whole complex; his father farms without much success and is not expected to rise. The boy grows up on the poor branch of a rich family, in a house where the accounts of a whiskey business are kept out loud. Under the fields around him lies the best coking coal anyone will find in America.
suggested_refs: The surviving Overholt homestead springhouse at West Overton, identified as the birthplace
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'
Wikipedia, 'West Overton, Pennsylvania'

stops.name: Mount Pleasant, thirty months of school
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; term dates unrecorded, defaulted to January. The pin marks the town of Mount Pleasant; the Institute building itself could not be located in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He is sent to the Mount Pleasant Institute, a few miles north of the family works, and stays long enough to be counted a pupil. It is one of only two schools he ever attends. His entire formal education, added across both of them and several interrupted terms, is later reckoned at about thirty months. He reads well, writes a clean hand, and is fast with figures. What the terms covered, and how many of them he sat through, no surviving account says. He is fourteen years old.
suggested_refs: Mount Pleasant Institute, Westmoreland County, one of the two schools Frick attended
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Westerville, ten weeks at Otterbein
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January. Coordinates corrected from the research pool, which placed the campus about 1.7 kilometres east of its actual site. The institution was named Otterbein University in 1866
stops.campa: He enrolls at Otterbein, a small United Brethren college in Ohio newly renamed a university, and leaves after roughly ten weeks with nothing to show. No account gives a reason. He is back in Westmoreland County before the term is out, and it is the last classroom he sits in as a student. For the rest of his life he will work among men who went to Yale and Princeton, hire them, and litigate against them. Whether he minded the difference is not something he ever wrote down.
suggested_refs: Otterbein University, Westerville, Ohio, attended for roughly ten weeks in 1866
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'
Wikipedia, 'Otterbein University'

stops.name: Broad Ford, the bookkeeper in his grandfather's distillery
stops.date_confidence: the sequence is corroborated in outline but sources differ on the order of the jobs and on his age at each; the year is approximate and month and day are defaulted to January
stops.campa: After clerking in relatives' stores and a spell selling in Pittsburgh, he takes the books at A. Overholt and Company, his grandfather's whiskey distillery at Broad Ford on the Youghiogheny. The ledger is his education: what a barrel costs, what it fetches, what the freight takes out of the difference. He is nineteen and already keeping his own separate accounts of what the coal in the district is doing. Sources differ on the order of these jobs and on how old he was at each. Decades later he will own the Overholt brand outright with Andrew Mellon, whose bank finances the coke.
suggested_refs: The A. Overholt and Company distillery buildings at West Overton and Broad Ford
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: The Connellsville district, fifty ovens at twenty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January. The pin marks the Connellsville coke district generally, not a single works
stops.campa: At twenty-one he goes into coke with Abraham O. Tintsman and Joseph Rist: three hundred acres of coal land and about fifty beehive ovens, under the name Frick and Company. He borrows against the ovens to build more ovens, then borrows against those, at a rate that alarms the bank in Pittsburgh. The beehive is a brick dome. Coal burns inside it for two days and comes out as coke, nearly pure carbon, the one fuel that will carry the weight of ore in a blast furnace. The domes stand in banks along the hillsides of the Connellsville field, smoking day and night.
suggested_refs: Surviving beehive coke oven banks of the Connellsville field
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: The Connellsville district, buying in the panic
stops.date_confidence: the Panic of 1873 and the railroad brokerage are attested; month and day defaulted to January. NPS and Wikipedia both date the buyout of the partnership to 'by 1880,' not 1879 as the research pool had it, and both put the first million at about age thirty
stops.campa: The Panic of 1873 closes banks, stops furnaces, and ruins coke men on every side of him. He does the reverse of what the ruined ones did: borrows more and buys their properties at panic prices, funded in part by some fifty thousand dollars he makes brokering the sale of a local railroad to the Baltimore and Ohio. Ovens bought for pennies are worth again what they were worth before, and then more. He buys out the partnership by 1880. Around his thirtieth birthday he is worth a million dollars and holds the Connellsville field.
suggested_refs: The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad purchase of the Mount Pleasant and Broad Ford line
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'
Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Oakland, the wedding at the Childs house
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinates corrected from the research pool, which sat about 250 metres north of the Forbes and Halket intersection
stops.campa: He marries Adelaide Howard Childs at her family's house at Forbes and Halket in Oakland, into a Pittsburgh merchant family with the standing coke money has not yet bought. The site will later hold Magee-Womens Hospital. In the same year he buys his first picture, a river landscape by George Hetzel, a Pittsburgh painter who taught half the artists in the county. There is no reason yet to think it is the beginning of anything. He is thirty-two years old.
suggested_refs: George Hetzel, Landscape with River, Frick's first documented art purchase
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'
The Frick Pittsburgh, 'The Courtship and Wedding of Henry and Adelaide'
The Frick Collection, Henry Clay Frick Art Collecting Files finding aid

stops.name: Point Breeze, the house called Clayton
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unrecorded and defaulted to the first. Coordinates corrected from the research pool, which fell about 950 metres west of the property, in Squirrel Hill
stops.campa: He pays about twenty-five thousand dollars for an eleven-room Italianate house on an acre and a half at Point Breeze, out where the Pittsburgh money is settling along the railroad. The address is 7227 Reynolds Street. The family moves in early in 1883 and the house takes the name Clayton. George Westinghouse lives up the road. Frick will hold it for the rest of his life and never give it up. Childs Frick is born here in March of 1883, Martha in August of 1885, Helen in September of 1888.
suggested_refs: Clayton, 7227 Reynolds Street, Pittsburgh
sources: Wikipedia, 'Clayton (Pittsburgh)'
The Frick Pittsburgh, historic-home research materials
frick.org, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: the coke company reorganized
stops.date_confidence: 1882 attested for the reorganization, autumn 1883 for the Carnegie majority; month and day of the reorganization unrecorded and defaulted to January. The pin is the downtown Fifth Avenue block of Frick's later office; no building is established for the 1882 transaction
stops.campa: He reorganizes the enterprise as the H. C. Frick Coke Company, some two million dollars of assets cut into forty thousand shares. Andrew Carnegie and his associates buy in, and by the autumn of 1883 the Carnegie interests hold the majority of the stock in Frick's own company. Frick keeps the management and the name. Carnegie needs coke and has no reliable supply of his own; Frick needs capital and a guaranteed buyer. The arrangement holds for sixteen years.
suggested_refs: The H. C. Frick Coke Company share ledgers, University of Pittsburgh, Henry Clay Frick Business Records
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Clayton, wired for current
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by The Frick Pittsburgh; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January. The claim that the house had electric light before the White House is the museum's own and is not independently verified here
stops.campa: Clayton is wired for electric light at the urging of his neighbor George Westinghouse, whose alternating-current works are a mile off; the museum's own account holds that the house had current before the White House did. There is a telephone in it, and central heat, and an alarm on the doors. Helen Clay Frick is born in September, the last of the four children and the one who will still be living in these rooms in the 1980s, with the furniture where her father left it.
suggested_refs: The Frick Pittsburgh, 'Clayton: A Modern High-tech Home'
sources: The Frick Pittsburgh, 'Clayton: A Modern High-tech Home'
Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Pittsburgh, chairman of Carnegie Brothers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Carnegie makes him chairman of Carnegie Brothers and Company and hands the daily command of the largest steel enterprise in America to the coke man from Westmoreland County. Frick sets about consolidating the scattered firms into what will be incorporated as the Carnegie Steel Company, buying up rivals and pulling ore, coke, rail, and mill into one line under one accounting. Carnegie spends much of the year abroad. The two men run the company between them by cable.
suggested_refs: The Carnegie-Frick correspondence, Frick Art Reference Library Archives
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, 'Henry Clay Frick'

segments.name: The Water, the Gas, and the Deputies

stops.name: South Fork, the club's lake comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested. The corpus text of Andrew Carnegie's file gives the death toll as 2,208 where the sources here give an official list of 2,209 and note estimates above 3,000; the discrepancy is left standing. Whether Frick personally co-owned or engineered the dam is disputed in the record, and club membership and promotion are the safest documented facts
stops.campa: Sixty miles east, above the steel town of Johnstown, an earthen dam holds back a lake stocked for the private pleasure of the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club. Frick is a founding and prominent member; so are Andrew Carnegie, Andrew Mellon, Philander Knox, and Henry Phipps. After days of rain the dam gives way and the lake comes down the valley in forty minutes. The official list of the dead runs to 2,209 names. Club lawyers, Knox and James Reed among them, defeat every liability suit brought against the members. No member pays anything.
suggested_refs: Johnstown Flood National Memorial, South Fork, Pennsylvania
The liability suits against the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, all defeated
sources: NPS, Johnstown Flood National Memorial, official site materials
Wikipedia, 'South Fork Dam'
andrew_carnegie.journey.json

stops.name: Mount Pleasant Township, the Mammoth mine
stops.date_confidence: date and operator attested. The death toll is disputed: the current Pennsylvania marker gives 109, one cited reference gives 118, and a federal industrial history gives 134. Not resolved. The research pool's place string, 'near Frick Park / Mammoth,' conflated this Westmoreland County mine with Frick Park in Pittsburgh some sixty kilometres away, and is corrected here
stops.campa: At the Mammoth No. 1 mine of the H. C. Frick Coke Company, gas ignites underground on a January morning while the shift is going in. The Pennsylvania marker at the site records 109 dead; a federal industrial history gives 134, and the count has never been settled. Seventy-nine of the bodies, unclaimed or beyond identifying, go into one grave at St. John the Baptist Cemetery in Scottdale. The company puts up a relief fund of twenty-five thousand dollars and tightens its rules underground. It is called the worst bituminous mine disaster in the state to that date.
suggested_refs: The mass grave of the Mammoth disaster, St. John the Baptist Cemetery, Scottdale
Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission marker, Mammoth Mine disaster
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mammoth Mine disaster'
Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission historical marker text

stops.name: Morewood, the deputies fire
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia dates the shooting to 30 March 1891 and gives nine dead; a Pennsylvania marker text and other accounts give 2 April and seven dead. Not resolved. The research pool originally attributed the shooting to National Guardsmen ordered in by Governor Robert Pattison; the Wikipedia account names Captain Loar and twelve county deputies and does not mention Pattison at all, and that attribution is corrected here. Coordinates likewise corrected by about 2.7 kilometres
stops.campa: Coke workers across the Connellsville field walk out over wages, and a column of about a thousand marchers moves on the Morewood works before dawn. Captain Loar and twelve county deputies fire into them. Nine miners die. Frick is not there, and no document has been found putting the order in his hand. He owns the works, refuses the strikers' terms, and keeps the ovens burning with men brought in from outside and guarded by Pinkertons, as he had with Hungarian and Slavic labor in 1884. The deputies are tried and acquitted. Whether anyone above them was ever asked is not in the record.
suggested_refs: The Morewood massacre marker, Westmoreland County, Pennsylvania
sources: Wikipedia, 'Morewood massacre'
PBS American Experience research on Homestead and the Pinkertons

stops.name: Clayton, Martha
stops.date_confidence: August 1891 attested; the exact day is not established in the sources consulted and is defaulted to the first. The Frick Pittsburgh does not state which house she died in; Clayton was the family home at the time
stops.campa: Martha Howard Frick dies a week short of her sixth birthday, after a long infection the family never fully accounts for. Her father buys the family lot at Homewood Cemetery the day after. He will have Daniel Burnham design the monument that stands over it, and the graves beneath it are marked with plain matching stones. The same season the house is torn apart and enlarged into a twenty-three-room, four-story thing in the Loire manner. Frick himself is laid up that year with rheumatoid arthritis, which recurs for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Frick lot, Section 14, Homewood Cemetery, monument by Daniel Burnham
sources: The Frick Pittsburgh, 'Disease and Illness in Gilded Age Pittsburgh, Part Two'
The Frick Pittsburgh, 'Memory and Mourning: A Frick History of Homewood Cemetery'
frick.org, 'Henry Clay Frick'

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: the union will not be met
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the exact day; the Library of Congress account places the announcement in the last week of June 1892. The Hussey Building no longer stands, so the pin approximates the downtown Fifth Avenue block
stops.campa: From his office on Fifth Avenue in Pittsburgh, Frick announces that Carnegie Steel will not deal with the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers as a union. The contract at the Homestead works expires at the end of the month. The company will treat with men one at a time or not at all. Andrew Carnegie, who has published essays friendly to organized labor and to the workman's right to combine, is in Scotland, and has left the handling of the contract to Frick. He stays there.
stops.quote: We could not confer with the Amalgamated Association officials.
stops.quote_source: Newspaper interview with H. C. Frick, entered as an exhibit and read into the record in Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, p. 32; the interview is from July 1892 and describes the position taken in June
suggested_refs: Library of Congress, 'This Month in Business History: 1892 Homestead Strike'
sources: Library of Congress, 'This Month in Business History: 1892 Homestead Strike'
explorepahistory.com marker 1-A-237
andrew_carnegie.journey.json

stops.name: Homestead, the fence with the rifle slots
stops.date_confidence: attested: the plate mill and one open hearth were locked on 28 June and the remainder on 29 June 1892. Coordinates inherited from the corpus pin for the Homestead Steel Works; the research pool's coordinates fell about 1.5 kilometres southwest, at the Homestead borough riverfront
stops.campa: The plate mill and one open hearth are shut on the twenty-eighth, the rest of the works on the twenty-ninth, and about three thousand eight hundred men are put out. They set their own pickets on the river bank and the rail line, and for a week nothing enters Homestead without the union's leave. Around the plant a solid board fence goes up, three miles long and twelve feet high, topped with barbed wire, pierced at intervals with slots at rifle height, searchlights on platforms above it. The men name it Fort Frick.
suggested_refs: The Bost Building, 621-623 East Eighth Avenue, Homestead, Amalgamated headquarters during the lockout
sources: PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'
Library of Congress, 'This Month in Business History: 1892 Homestead Strike'
andrew_carnegie.journey.json

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: the letter to the superintendent
stops.date_confidence: attested and dated; the letter was read by Frick himself into the record of the House Judiciary Committee investigation
stops.campa: Four days before the barges are due he writes to John A. Potter, his general superintendent at Homestead, about the guards the company is bringing in. The letter is careful in one particular way: it does not instruct Potter, it tells him what he no doubt already fully realizes about staying inside the law. Some three hundred armed men are at that moment being gathered in other states and moved toward the Ohio River under the name of watchmen. Six months later Frick reads this letter aloud to a committee of Congress.
stops.quote: I have no doubt you fully realize the importance of not doing anything or permitting anything to be done by any of our employes, or any guards we may employ, to protect our property that is not entirely lawful.
stops.quote_source: Letter from H. C. Frick, Chairman, to John A. Potter, general superintendent, 2 July 1892, read into the record in Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, p. 36
suggested_refs: U.S. House Report 2447, 'Employment of Pinkerton Detectives,' 52nd Congress, 2nd Session (1893)
sources: Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, testimony of H. C. Frick, p. 36 (Internet Archive OCR text)

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: the letter to the sheriff
stops.date_confidence: attested and dated; the letter was read by Frick himself into the record of the House Judiciary Committee investigation
stops.campa: On Independence Day he writes to Sheriff W. H. McCleary of Allegheny County. Bodies of men have collected at and around the works in Mifflin Township and on the highways leading to them from all directions, preventing the company's employees from getting in or out. He calls on the sheriff to protect the property from violence, damage, and destruction, and to protect the company in the free use and enjoyment of it. The civil authority has now been asked, formally and in writing. The sheriff has no force able to do any of it. Two days later the barges start upriver.
stops.quote: Will you please take notice that at and in the vicinity of our works in Mifflin Township, near Homestead, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, and upon the highways leading thereto from all directions, bodies of men have collected who assume to and do prevent to our employes access to and egress from our property... We therefore call upon you, as sheriff of Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, to protect our property from violence, damage, and destruction, and to protect us in its free use and enjoyment.
stops.quote_source: Frick, as Chairman of The Carnegie Steel Co., Ld., to Sheriff W. H. McCleary, 4 July 1892, read into his sworn testimony, Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, p. 36
suggested_refs: U.S. House Report 2447, 'Employment of Pinkerton Detectives,' 52nd Congress, 2nd Session (1893)
sources: Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, testimony of H. C. Frick, pp. 36-39 (Internet Archive OCR text)

stops.name: Homestead, the barges at the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested. Who fired first is unresolved in every source consulted, and casualty counts vary slightly between accounts; seven workers and three Pinkertons is the figure common to the accounts used here
stops.campa: About three hundred Pinkerton men, hired as watchmen and issued rifles, are towed up the Monongahela on two barges in the dark and reach the mill landing near four in the morning. The town is awake and waiting, a whistle having gone off downriver. Shooting starts at the gangplank and nobody has ever established who fired first. It runs some twelve hours: rifle fire from behind steel plate, burning oil floated down onto the barges, a cannon dragged up the bank. Seven workers and three Pinkertons die. The detectives surrender and are beaten as they come ashore through the crowd.
suggested_refs: The Pinkerton landing site, Homestead, designated by the Pittsburgh History and Landmarks Foundation in 1989
sources: PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'
Library of Congress, 'This Month in Business History: 1892 Homestead Strike'
Rivers of Steel and Zinn Education Project accounts of the Battle of Homestead

stops.name: Clayton, a son born in the crisis
stops.date_confidence: the birth date is attested; the birthplace is reconstruction. Family-history material places the birth within days of the lockout but does not establish that it happened at Clayton rather than elsewhere, and Clayton's pin is used on that basis
stops.campa: Two days after the battle at the landing, Adelaide gives birth to a son, named Henry Clay Frick Jr. The mother does not recover well. The child lives a few weeks and dies of causes the record does not name. His father spends those weeks running a lockout under armed guard, with the state militia on the way and the newspapers of two continents printing his name daily. The boy goes into the ground at Homewood beside his sister, in the lot bought eleven months before.
suggested_refs: The Frick family lot, Section 14, Homewood Cemetery
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'
The Frick Pittsburgh family-history material (cited via the research dossier, not independently fetched)

stops.name: Homestead, the militia on the high ground
stops.date_confidence: 12 July 1892 attested, with Major General George R. Snowden in command. Troop strength is given as roughly 6,000 in the source consulted here, better than 4,000 in the town with about 2,000 more camped above it; the figure of 8,500 circulates in other accounts, including the corpus text of Andrew Carnegie's file, and is not resolved
stops.campa: Governor Robert Pattison, who has put the company off for two weeks, orders out the Pennsylvania National Guard. Major General George Snowden brings better than four thousand soldiers into Homestead on the twelfth, with something like two thousand more camped on the high ground above the town. The union meets them with a brass band and a welcoming address and is ignored. Under military protection the company begins moving replacement workers in by rail and by river and houses them inside the fence. The mill starts up again.
suggested_refs: Pennsylvania National Guard orders and returns for the Homestead deployment, July 1892
sources: Wikipedia, 'Homestead strike'
PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: Berkman at the office door
stops.date_confidence: attested, and corroborated by a contemporary Los Angeles Herald report of 24 July 1892. The account that Frick finished the day's work before letting a surgeon in is stated as fact in the corpus text of Andrew Carnegie's file and is widely repeated; no contemporaneous medical record was located. The related tradition that he refused anesthesia during the extraction of the bullets is likewise unverified and is not asserted here
stops.campa: A young Russian-born anarchist named Alexander Berkman, who has never been to Homestead and knows no one in it, talks his way into the office and shoots Frick twice, then stabs him three times with a sharpened file. Frick shouts, and by Berkman's own account the words are Murder! Help! A vice-chairman and a passing carpenter get the man down, the carpenter with a hammer. Bleeding on the floor, Frick tells the police not to shoot him. He is said to have stayed at his desk until the day's letters were finished.
stops.quote: Don't shoot. Leave him to the law.
stops.quote_source: Frick to the arriving police, his Pittsburgh office, 23 July 1892, as given in Wikipedia, 'Alexander Berkman'
suggested_refs: Alexander Berkman, Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist (Mother Earth, 1912), ch. IV, 'The Attentat,' p. 34
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'
Wikipedia, 'Alexander Berkman'
Alexander Berkman, Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist (1912), p. 34

stops.name: Clayton, the answer given from the bed
stops.date_confidence: attested and now traced to its primary source: Milholland's written report of the interview, forwarded by Whitelaw Reid to President Harrison and printed in George Harvey's 1928 biography, p. 151. The research pool carried the line with a bare July 1892 date on PBS's secondary rendering; the exact date and the setting come from Harvey
stops.campa: A week after the shooting, John E. Milholland comes to the house on an errand for Whitelaw Reid, the Republican candidate for vice president, whose ticket is being buried under Homestead in the middle of a presidential campaign. Frick is in bed, his face and head swathed in bandages. Milholland asks him how long the thing is going to go on. He writes the answer down and sends it to Reid, who forwards it to President Harrison. The words reach print thirty-six years later, in the authorized biography.
stops.quote: if it takes all summer and all winter, and all next summer and all next winter. Yes, even my life itself. I will fight this thing to the bitter end. I will never recognize the Union, never, never!
stops.quote_source: Frick to John E. Milholland at Frick's house, 30 July 1892, in Milholland's report to Whitelaw Reid, printed in George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (Scribner's, 1928), p. 151
suggested_refs: George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (Scribner's, 1928), chapter 'Politics'
sources: George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (1928), p. 151 (Internet Archive, henryclayfrickth001433mbp)
PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'

stops.name: Allegheny County, Berkman sentenced
stops.date_confidence: September 1892 attested for the conviction; day unrecorded and defaulted to the first. The sentence is reported inconsistently: contemporary sources give 22 years, later accounts commonly cite roughly 14 years served before release in 1906. Not resolved
stops.campa: Berkman is tried in Allegheny County and sent to the penitentiary. He had never worked in a steel mill and knew nobody at Homestead; he believed the deed would speak for itself to the men there. It did not. The workers repudiated him within the day, and the strike leaders spent the following week telling reporters they had no anarchists among them. Public sympathy for the locked-out men drains away that summer and does not come back. Emma Goldman, who helped plan the attempt, is never charged.
suggested_refs: Alexander Berkman, Prison Memoirs of an Anarchist (1912), on the trial and the Western Penitentiary
sources: Wikipedia, 'Henry Clay Frick'
Web-search sources on Berkman's sentence and his 1906 release

stops.name: Fifth Avenue, Pittsburgh: the cable to Scotland
stops.date_confidence: both telegrams attested and dated in the Carnegie-Frick correspondence as reproduced by PBS, verified from the raw page text. The 31 October letter is attested in Harvey, p. 177, and postdates the battle; it is not evidence of Frick's intentions before the lockout
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of November he cables Carnegie a single word: Victory. On the twentieth the men vote to go back, those the company will take back, and the leaders are blacklisted. Three weeks earlier he had written to Carnegie that Homestead had never been well managed and that the mills had never turned out the product they should, being held back by the Amalgamated men. That letter is dated the thirty-first of October, after the barges and after the militia. On the twenty-first he writes again.
stops.quote: Strike officially declared off yesterday. Our victory is now complete and most gratifying. Do not think we will ever have any serious labor trouble again.... Let the Amalgamated still exist and hold full sway at other people's mills. That is no concern of ours.
stops.quote_source: Telegram from Frick to Andrew Carnegie, 21 November 1892, Carnegie-Frick correspondence, reproduced by PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'
suggested_refs: The Carnegie-Frick telegrams of November 1892
George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (1928), p. 177, for the letter of 31 October 1892
sources: PBS American Experience, 'The Strike at Homestead Mill'
George Harvey, Henry Clay Frick: The Man (1928), p. 177

stops.name: Washington, sworn before the committee
stops.date_confidence: the investigation ran across the winter of 1892-93 and its report, House Report 2447, 52nd Congress, 2nd Session, was printed in 1893; the exact day of Frick's appearance is not established in the material consulted, so the date is set to the year. The pin is the Capitol: the record establishes sworn testimony before the House Judiciary Committee but not the room
stops.campa: A committee of the House of Representatives investigates the employment of Pinkerton detectives in the Homestead troubles, and Frick is sworn. He reads his own letters into the record, the one to Potter and the one to the sheriff, and enters a newspaper interview in which he had said the company could not confer with Amalgamated officials, would protect its property at all hazards, and had never given a thought to what its affairs might do to either political party. Asked what the Pinkerton men were for, he answers: only to protect our property.
stops.quote: We did not bring in a body of armed men.
stops.quote_source: H. C. Frick, sworn testimony, Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, p. 39
suggested_refs: U.S. House Report 2447, 'Employment of Pinkerton Detectives,' 52nd Congress, 2nd Session (1893), the largest printed body of Frick's own words
sources: Investigation of the Employment of Pinkerton Detectives at Homestead, Pa., House Judiciary Committee, testimony of H. C. Frick, pp. 32-39 (Internet Archive OCR text)

stops.name: Pittsburgh, the chairmanship resigned
stops.date_confidence: attested by the University of Pittsburgh finding aid for the Frick business records; the 1897 mediation by James H. Reed is attested by The Frick Pittsburgh
stops.campa: The partnership has been coming apart for years. In 1897 the attorney James H. Reed had to mediate a truce between them. The quarrel is over the price of coke, which Frick sells to Carnegie Steel and also to everybody else, and underneath that it is over which of the two men is the principal. On the fifth of December Frick resigns the chairmanship. Carnegie then moves to force him out of his shares under the iron-clad agreement the partners had all signed. The instrument values a departing partner's interest at book value, nothing like what it is worth.

stops.name: Allegheny County, Frick against Carnegie
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He files in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas against Andrew Carnegie, asking that the iron-clad agreement be set aside, and the pleadings put the books of Carnegie Steel into a public record for the first time. The profits in them are enormous, larger than anyone outside the partnership had guessed, and they are printed in newspapers all over the country within days. Carnegie has spent a decade explaining the duties of wealth in magazines. His own counsel starts advising a settlement.

stops.name: Atlantic City, the settlement out of court
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested and the city is named in the source, which gives neither a date nor a building for the meeting. The month and day here are a placeholder chosen only to order the segment after the February filing and carry no evidentiary weight
stops.campa: The suit never reaches a verdict. The parties meet at Atlantic City and settle, and the whole apparatus is reorganized: Carnegie Steel and the H. C. Frick Coke Company are folded into a new Carnegie Company of New Jersey, with Frick's interest recognized at something near what it was actually worth. He walks out holding shares valued inside two years at better than thirty million dollars. He is fifty years old. The two men never work together again, and no letter of reconciliation between them has been found.

Frick, holding what Atlantic City gave him, takes a seat on the board and no longer runs anything. Two years on, Theodore Roosevelt asks him to join the Isthmian Canal Commission and he declines. stops.name: Italy, the passage they did not take

stops.campa: They travel in Europe most years now, the dealers and the sale rooms as much as the scenery, and a return crossing is booked the way another man books a train. This spring Adelaide turns her ankle badly in Italy and needs a hospital, and the Fricks give up the passage they had taken home on a new ship's maiden voyage. The Titanic sails without them in April and goes down on the fourth night out. The story attaches itself to the family afterward, retold as a near miss and a sign. Nothing in the record suggests anything but the ankle.

It is designed from the start to become a museum: rooms sized to pictures, an interior court, a gallery wing, daylight handled the way a curator would want it handled rather than the way a family would. The Lenox Library is demolished to clear the site. He is sixty-three when the ground is broken.

Adelaide takes her floor above; the galleries are below; the collection hangs where strangers will one day walk past it. Frick is sixty-four. Pittsburgh is four hundred miles behind him, the ovens still burning under his name and the mill still running behind its fence. He has five years to live in the house.

stops.campa: At Knoedler's rooms at 556 Fifth Avenue he buys Vermeer's Mistress and Maid: a woman at a table in yellow, a servant handing her a letter, the whole exchange stopped at the instant before the letter is read. Thirty-eight years back down the same line of purchases is a Pittsburgh coke clerk paying for a river landscape by George Hetzel, and between the two stand the ovens, the fence, the barges, and the settlement at Atlantic City. The Vermeer is in the house by the end of the year. He is sixty-nine and still opening what the dealers send.

stops.campa: The body goes back to Pittsburgh by rail and into the lot in Section 14 of Homewood Cemetery that he bought the day after Martha died, twenty-eight years earlier. stops.name: One East Seventieth Street, the doors opened
stops.date_confidence: attested, including the soft opening for 700 invited visitors on 11 December 1935
stops.campa: Adelaide dies in 1931 and the house becomes what the will said it would become. John Russell Pope converts it, adding a garden court and gallery space, and on the eleventh of December seven hundred invited people walk the rooms. On the sixteenth the doors open to anybody with the price of admission. Sixteen years after his death, a stranger can stand in Henry Clay Frick's living room and look at his Vermeers. In 2020 the collection closes for renovation, spends three years in the old Whitney building on Madison Avenue, and returns to Fifth Avenue in April of 2025.

stops.name: Clayton, the house reopened and the legacy reopened
stops.date_confidence: 1990 opening, the 2013-2015 renovation, and the May 2025 National Register listing are attested; month and day of the 1990 opening are unrecorded and defaulted to January. The institutional reexamination of Frick's legacy is documented for 2020-2023
stops.campa: Helen Clay Frick dies in 1984 having lived in the Pittsburgh house nearly all her life, and in 1990 it opens as a museum with the family's own furniture still standing where they left it. A car and carriage museum goes up alongside, rebuilt for fifteen million dollars between 2013 and 2015, and the National Register lists the house in May of 2025. By the early 2020s the institution is running exhibitions and programs on its founder's fraught legacy, the lockout and the Pinkerton barges named plainly. The house stands at the edge of the Homewood neighborhood.
